blocks.content: Imagine your teammate is writing a unit test for OrderService. They create an InMemoryOrderRepository and pass it to the service so the test can run without a real database. But the test still tries to connect to PostgreSQL.
The reason is simple: OrderService ignores the repository that was provided and creates its own PostgresOrderRepositoryinternally.
You fixed one problem by introducing an interface, but the class is still deciding which implementation to use. The code is still tightly coupled and difficult to test.

Dependency Injection solves this problem by moving the responsibility of creating dependencies outside the class. The class simply receives a ready-to-use dependency and focuses only on its business logic.

Real-Life Analogy

Think of a laptop charger. The laptop doesn't generate its own electricity. It simply has a power plug and expects electricity to be provided.

The electricity might come from a wall socket, a generator, or a battery backup. The laptop doesn't know and doesn't care where it came from.

Dependency Injection works the same way. A class should not create its own dependencies. It should simply declare what it needs and let someone else provide it. This makes the class easier to test, easier to change, and much more flexible.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 1. What is dependency injection

Dependency injection is a technique where an object receives the other objects it depends on from an external source typically passed into its constructor, a setter method, or a method parameter rather than creating those dependencies itself internally.

The class declares what it needs, usually as an interface or abstract type, and something outside the class calling code, a test, or a dedicated dependency injection framework is responsible for constructing the concrete dependency and handing it over.

This is what makes the dependency inversion principle from the coupling and cohesion lesson actually achievable in practice: depending on an abstraction only fully decouples a class if that class also never constructs the concrete implementation of that abstraction itself.
2. The three ways a dependency can be injected
blocks.text: 2. The three ways a dependency can be injected

blocks.content: Dependency Injection can happen in three different ways, depending on when and how the dependency is provided to the object.
blocks.text: Dependency Injection can happen in three different ways, depending on when and how the dependency is provided to the object.

blocks.content: 1. Constructor Injection
Dependencies are passed through the constructor when the object is created.
The object cannot exist without these dependencies, so they are guaranteed to be available throughout its lifetime. This is the most common and recommended approach for required dependencies.
When to use: When a dependency is mandatory and the object cannot work without it.
2. Setter Injection
Dependencies are provided after the object has already been created through setter methods.
This means the object can exist without the dependency for some time, making the dependency optional or configurable later.
When to use: When a dependency is optional or may change after object creation.
3. Interface Injection
The class implements a specific interface, and the dependency injection framework calls a method defined by that interface to provide the dependency.
The class becomes aware of the injection mechanism because it must implement the injection interface.
When to use: Rarely used today. Mostly found in older frameworks before constructor injection became the standard approach.

blocks.content: Fix in code

The fix is small in terms of lines changed, but the consequence is large:OrderService went from a class that always decides its own dependency to a class that has an opinion about what kind of thing it needs  anOrderRepository with zero opinion about which specific implementation shows up.
The decision moved to exactly one place, called the composition root, which is the only part of the system that's allowed to know about concrete classes likePostgresOrderRepositoryat all.

items: It completes Dependency Inversion: Depending on an interface alone is not enough. If a class still creates the concrete implementation itself, it remains tightly coupled. Dependency Injection completes Dependency Inversion by moving the creation of dependencies outside the class.

It makes the Repository Pattern truly swappable: The OrderRepository interface becomes useful only when something else decides which implementation to provide. Otherwise, switching from PostgreSQL to an in-memory repository still requires changing the service code.

It is Composition at construction time: Composition means one object holds another object instead of inheriting from it. Dependency Injection answers the next question: who creates that object and passes it in? The answer is an external component.

blocks.content: 4. Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Depending on an interface but creating the concrete class internally
A class may accept an OrderRepository but still call new PostgresOrderRepository() inside. This defeats the purpose of Dependency Injection because the dependency is still hardcoded.
Mistake 2: Injecting too many dependencies
If a constructor needs eight or nine dependencies, the class is probably doing too many things. The solution is usually to split the class into smaller responsibilities.
Mistake 3: Composition logic scattered everywhere
If multiple places in the code decide which repository implementation to create, changing that implementation later becomes difficult. Object creation should happen in one central place.
Mistake 4: Using a DI framework too early

For small applications, manual dependency injection is often simpler and easier to understand. Dependency Injection frameworks become valuable only when wiring a large number of objects manually becomes difficult.
5. Quick Reference

["Principle: A class receives its dependencies from outside and never creates them itself.
","Power Cord Analogy: A device with a power cord doesn't care where electricity comes from; it simply uses it.
","Constructor Injection: The recommended approach where dependencies are passed through the constructor.
","Composition Root: The single place responsible for creating and wiring all objects together.
","Dependency Inversion + DI: A class becomes fully decoupled only when it depends on an abstraction and stops creating the implementation itself.
","Frameworks: Start with manual injection and introduce a DI framework only when the application's size and complexity justify it."]
